analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for companies to classify workers as independent contractors outside minimum wage, overtime, and union protections.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House committee on a 19-16 vote and has sat on the House floor calendar since February 2026, with no floor vote and no Senate action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes a narrow test into federal labor law for deciding who counts as an independent contractor rather than an employee. Under the bill, a worker is a contractor if the company does not control the details of how the work gets done and the worker bears entrepreneurial-style opportunity and risk. It also forbids counting a company's requirements that workers follow laws, meet stricter health and safety standards, carry insurance, or hit deadlines as evidence that someone is an employee. Because federal minimum wage, overtime, and union rights apply only to employees [S2], more workers classified as contractors means fewer people covered by those protections.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that rely on contract labor gain the most: gig platforms, franchisors, staffing intermediaries, and any business that wants to avoid paying overtime or minimum wage, or that wants to keep contract workers out of union bargaining. The bill gives these companies a statutory standard, meaning a rule written by Congress that courts must follow, instead of leaving classification to the Labor Department and courts. Some workers who genuinely run independent businesses would benefit from a clearer, more predictable rule.

how_it_helps.text: Gives companies a two-part statutory test for treating workers as independent contractors: no significant control over the details of the work, plus entrepreneurial opportunity and risk [S2] [S3].

Bars consideration of whether a company requires workers to comply with laws, meet stricter health and safety standards, carry insurance, or meet contract deadlines when deciding their status [S2] [S3].
Applies the same narrow standard to the National Labor Relations Act, so workers classified as contractors are also excluded from federal collective bargaining rights [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who are classified as contractors under the new standard lose the federal minimum wage, overtime pay, and collective bargaining rights, which under federal law apply exclusively to employees [S2]. Because a company can require workers to follow laws, carry insurance, and hit deadlines without that counting as control, a worker can be under a company's thumb in practice while counted as a contractor under the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers shifted out of employee status

drawbacks.text: Workers reclassified as contractors are excluded from minimum wage, overtime, and collective bargaining protections, which federal labor laws apply exclusively to employees [S2].

The bill forbids counting requirements to follow laws, meet stronger health and safety standards, carry insurance, or meet deadlines as evidence of employment [S3], so a company can dictate many terms of a worker's job while still treating the person as a contractor.

A good-faith objection from supporters of the bill: federal regulators' broader tests can sweep genuinely self-employed professionals, tradespeople, and freelancers into employee status against their will, and the bill is pitched as protecting independent work. The honest cost is that the same standard also lets large companies move employees out of wage and union protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives real clarity to genuinely independent workers, but its main practical effect is to lower the bar for companies to classify workers as contractors and to strip from that calculation the very requirements, like deadlines, insurance, and safety rules, that often show a company controls the work. The people most affected, workers moved out of employee status, lose minimum wage, overtime, and union rights, while the businesses that make the classification decision gain flexibility and lower labor costs. On balance, the gains flow to companies far more than to the workers the bill's name invokes.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee approved it 19-16 in July 2025 and formally reported it to the floor in February 2026, where it now sits on the House calendar awaiting action; the Senate has not touched it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 13, 2025, by Rep. Kevin Kiley and referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce [S1] [S5].
The committee held a markup and voted 19-16 on July 23, 2025, to order the bill reported with an amendment [S5].
The committee formally reported the bill on February 20, 2026, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the House floor calendar, as Calendar No. 431 [S3] [S5].
No floor vote has taken place in the House, and the bill has no Senate counterpart action in the record [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill is not law, no one has won yet. If it stalls, the beneficiaries are workers who would have lost minimum wage, overtime, and union protections; the bill's advancement to the House calendar, however, moves contractor-reliant companies closer to a statutory standard written in their favor.

for.name: Kevin Kiley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided it through the Education and Workforce Committee to House floor calendar placement.

for.name: 23 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.

for.name: Gig-economy platforms
for.what_they_did: Have publicly pushed for a federal standard that locks in independent-contractor status for their drivers, the outcome this bill's test would produce.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against reporting the bill; the panel advanced it on a close 19-16 vote.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor is a House Republican, no Democrat signed on, and the committee reported it on a narrow 19-16 vote, a margin consistent with a partisan split [S4] [S5].

industries.note: A statutory two-factor test that ignores control over scheduling, safety rules, insurance, and deadlines makes it far harder to classify their workers as employees. That spares the companies the cost of minimum wage, overtime, and benefits funded by employers, costs that would otherwise fall on them rather than on workers or taxpayers.

Companies that structure work through contract and franchise relationships gain a federal rule of decision that shields their classifications. Workers in these chains lose employee-status protections like the wage floor and overtime [S2].

industries.industry: Organized labor and unionized employers' bargaining units
industries.note: Applying the same narrow test to the National Labor Relations Act excludes contractors from collective bargaining, shrinking the pool of workers who can organize and bargain.
A predictable statutory test reduces the risk that independent professionals are swept into employee status by broader regulatory tests, giving them certainty about their status.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been on the House floor calendar since February 2026 without a scheduled vote, has only Republican support in the House, and has no movement in the Senate. Bills that clear committee but wait months on the calendar with purely partisan backing and no Senate companion typically die when the Congress ends; it would need House leadership to schedule a floor vote and the Senate to act, neither of which the record shows happening.
